title: Moon landing
summary: This document is a comprehensive article on Moon landings (lunar landings), covering both crewed and robotic spacecraft arrivals on the Moon. It begins with an overview of lunar landing history, from the first hard landing by Luna 2 in 1959 through the first crewed landing by Apollo 11 in 1969, and notes recent achievements including China's Chang'e missions, India's Chandrayaan-3, Japan's SLIM, and commercial landings by Intuitive Machines and Firefly Aerospace. The article details uncrewed landings by six government space agencies (Interkosmos, NASA, CNSA, ISRO, JAXA, and ESA) as well as commercial efforts, including both failures (Beresheet, Hakuto-R) and successes (Odysseus, Blue Ghost). It covers crewed landings accomplished by twelve Apollo astronauts between 1969 and 1972. The document explains the scientific background of lunar landings, including escape velocity, delta-v requirements, hard versus soft landing techniques, and the engineering challenges of lunar departure and Earth return. It provides political context surrounding the Cold War Space Race, including Sputnik's launch, U.S. and Soviet strategies, the Kennedy administration's decision to pursue Apollo, and the Soviet N1/Zond efforts. The article chronologically traces early Soviet and American uncrewed missions (1958–1965), including Pioneer and Ranger programs; first soft landings by Luna 9, Surveyor, and the Lunokhod rovers; the transition to lunar orbit operations and discovery of mascons; and Soviet circumlunar Zond flights. It then details the Apollo program missions, subsequent deliberate crash landings of orbiters (Hiten, Lunar Prospector, SMART-1, LCROSS, GRAIL, LADEE, and others), and 21st-century soft landings and attempts by China (Chang'e 3–6), Israel, India, Japan, Russia, and the U.S. commercial sector. Finally, it briefly covers landings on moons of other Solar System bodies (such as Huygens on Titan) and proposed future missions, including NASA's Artemis program, China's International Lunar Research Station plans, and missions by ISRO/JAXA and Roscosmos.
